{{Short description|Rugby union club competition}} {{about|the men's rugby union tournament in the Pacific region|the pan-American men's tournament|Super Rugby Americas|the women's tournament in Australia and Fiji|Super Rugby Women's|the women's tournament in New Zealand|Super Rugby Aupiki|the men's tournament in Brazil|Brazilian Rugby Union Championship}} {{EngvarB|date=November 2015}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2026}} {{Infobox sports league | title = Super Rugby | current_season = 2026 Super Rugby Pacific season | logo = Super Rugby Pacific logo.png | logo_upright = 0.7 | formerly = {{plainlist| * Super 12 (1996–2005) * Super 14 (2006–2010) }} | last_season = | upcoming_season = | sport = Rugby union | founded = {{start date and age|1996}} | folded = | replaced = | owner = [[SANZAAR]] | ceo = Jack Mesley | first = [[1996 Super 12 season|1996]] | teams = [[#Current franchises|10]] | country = {{plainlist| * Australia (4 teams) * [[Fiji]] (1 team) * New Zealand (5 teams) }} | champion = {{rut|Hurricanes}} | champ_season = [[2026 Super Rugby Pacific season|2026]], 2nd title | most_titles = [[Crusaders (rugby union)|Crusaders]] (13 titles) | broadcaster = See [[#Broadcasters|broadcasters]] | related_comps = {{plainlist| * [[Super Rugby Women's]] * [[Super Rugby Aupiki]] }} | founder = | website = [https://super.rugby/superrugby/ super.rugby] }} '''Super Rugby''' is a men's professional [[rugby union]] club competition involving teams from Australia, Fiji, New Zealand, and the Pacific Islands. It has previously included teams from Argentina, Japan, and South Africa. Super Rugby started as the '''Super 12''' in the [[1996 Super 12 season|1996 season]] with 12 teams from Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa, building on competitions dating back to the [[South Pacific Championship]] in 1986. The Super 12 was established by [[SANZAAR|SANZAR]] after the sport became professional in 1995. After the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] forced the competition to split into three, the reformed competition in 2021 only included teams from Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific islands. The name was changed to '''Super 14''' with the addition of two teams for the [[2006 Super 14 season|2006 season]], and with expansion to 15 teams for the [[2011 Super Rugby season|2011 season]], the competition was rebranded as Super Rugby (with no number). In 2016 two new teams, the [[Jaguares (Super Rugby)|Jaguares]] from Argentina and [[Sunwolves]] from Japan, joined the competition, playing in two newly separated African groups. In 2018, the Cheetahs, Kings and Western Force were dropped, leaving 15 teams. The Sunwolves left the competition before the end of the 2020 season. The 2020 season was cancelled due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].{{Cite web|date=15 March 2020|title=Super Rugby 2020 season shut down: Coronavirus news, SANZAAR, Highlanders vs Jaguares cancelled, NZ travel restriction|url=https://www.foxsports.com.au/rugby/super-rugby/super-rugby-sanzaar-competition-to-be-halted-for-the-foreseeable-future/news-story/9793242c08bab0fe2b232f011699e28c|access-date=27 December 2020|website=Fox Sports|language=en-AU}} Due to international travel restrictions relating to the pandemic, [[Rugby Australia]] and [[New Zealand Rugby]] held domestic tournaments, [[Super Rugby AU]] and [[Super Rugby Aotearoa]] respectively.{{Cite web|title=Suncorp Stadium derby to open Super Rugby AU competition|url=https://www.rugby.com.au/news/2020/06/10/super-rugby-au-confirmation|access-date=27 December 2020|website=www.rugby.com.au|date=10 June 2020 |language=en}}{{Cite web|title=Investec Super Rugby Aotearoa ready to kick off in June|url=https://superrugby.co.nz/news/investec-super-rugby-aotearoa-ready-to-kick-off-in-june/|access-date=27 December 2020|website=superrugby.co.nz|date=11 May 2020 |language=en-GB}} Both these tournaments continued in 2021, to be followed by [[Super Rugby Trans-Tasman]], a crossover tournament.{{Cite web|title=2021 set for thrilling Trans-Tasman crossover|url=https://www.rugby.com.au/news/2020/11/12/2021-set-for-thrilling-trans-tasman-crossover|access-date=27 December 2020|website=www.rugby.com.au|date=12 November 2020 |language=en}} In September 2020, the [[South African Rugby Union]] withdrew their four franchises from the competition, with plans for them to join the [[United Rugby Championship|PRO14]].{{Cite web|title=SARU members vote to seek northern hemisphere future|url=https://www.sarugby.co.za//news-features/articles/2020/09/29/saru-members-vote-to-seek-northern-hemisphere-future/|access-date=27 December 2020|website=SA Rugby}} The Argentine [[Jaguares (Super Rugby)|Jaguares]] also left the competition. In August 2021 a 12-team format was confirmed, with the addition of the Fijian Drua and Moana Pasifika, a team representing the [[Pacific Islands]]. The tournament from 2022 is named '''Super Rugby Pacific'''.{{Cite web|title=Reports: Agreement reached for 12-team Super Rugby from 2022|url=https://www.sarugbymag.co.za/super-rugby-set-twelve-2022/|access-date=27 December 2020|website=www.sarugbymag.co.za|date=4 November 2020 }}{{cite news|url=https://www.rugby.com.au/news/super-rugby-pacific-new-format-teams-structure-2021829|title=RA, NZR launch new era with formation of Super Rugby Pacific|work=Rugby.com.au|date=30 August 2021|access-date=30 August 2021}} The competition has been dominated by New Zealand teams, who have won 21 times in 28 years. The {{Rut|Crusaders}} have won most often, with 13 titles. == Organisation and format == === SANZAAR === {{Main|SANZAAR}} [[SANZAAR]] is the body that administers Super Rugby, and has the [[Australian Rugby Union|Australian]], [[New Zealand Rugby Union|New Zealand]], [[South African Rugby Union|South African]] and [[Argentine Rugby Union|Argentine]] rugby unions as its members. SANZAAR also runs the [[The Rugby Championship|Rugby Championship]] tournament that is contested by [[Argentina national rugby union team|Argentina]], [[Australia national rugby union team|Australia]], [[New Zealand national rugby union team|New Zealand]] and [[South Africa national rugby union team|South Africa]] following the conclusion of the Super Rugby tournament; the Tri-Nations preceded the Rugby Championship before Argentina joined the competition. The organisation was formed in 1996 to establish and run the Super 12, and Tri-Nations Tournament. === Competition format === {{Wide image|Force Rugby Kickoff.jpg|700|[[Western Force]] (Blue) kicking off to the [[New South Wales Waratahs]] (White).}} Prior to 2011, Super Rugby was a [[Round-robin tournament|round-robin]] competition where each team played every other team once; a team had six or seven home games, and six or seven away games each. The winner received four competition points; if the game was a draw two points were awarded to each team. The [[Rugby union bonus points system|bonus points system]] was also used, where any team scoring four or more tries, and/or losing by seven points or less, receives an extra competition point. In 2016, the try bonus changed. A team now has to score three more tries than their opponents. The top four teams at the end of the round-robin phase then played semi-finals – the first placed team hosting the fourth placed team, and the second placed team hosting the third placed team.{{cite web| url=http://www.planetrugby.com/Story/0,18259,9991_1745267,00.html |title=Super 12: The History |publisher=planetrugby.com |access-date=16 April 2007 |date=24 May 2001}} The two winners then played the final at the home ground of the top surviving seed. There were 91 [[regular season]] games in total.{{cite web |url=http://www.super14.com/fixtures/2007fixturesLGMT.asp |publisher=super14.com |title=2007 Super 14 Fixtures |access-date=16 April 2007 |archive-date=30 September 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080930202005/http://www.super14.com/fixtures/2007fixturesLGMT.asp |url-status=dead }} Games were held over 14 weekends with each team receiving one [[Bye (sports)|bye]]. From [[Super rugby 2011|2011]] – 2015 the format changed, with each country forming its own [[Athletic conference|conference]]. Each team within a conference played each of the other teams in its conference twice, once at home and once away. Each team then played four out of the five teams from each of the other conferences once. Competition points were awarded on a similar basis as before. The format of the finals also changed; it involved six teams: the top team in each of the three conferences plus the three next teams with the highest total number of points, regardless of conference. The four lower ranking teams were paired in two sudden death games; the winners of those two games each played one of the two top ranked teams (which received a bye at the start of the finals). Those winners played for the championship.{{cite web |publisher=Sports Digital Media |url=http://www.superxv.com/format/ |title=Super XV Rugby Format | Super Rugby News, Results and Fixtures from Super XV Rugby |via=Superxv.com |access-date=23 February 2012 |archive-date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414094134/http://www.superxv.com/format/ |url-status=dead }} For the [[Super rugby 2016|2016]] and 2017 seasons the format changed again, with three more teams joining, one each from Argentina, Japan and South Africa. There were four conferences, with Africa getting two conferences. The finals had eight teams with each conference winner getting a home quarter final. They were joined by four wild card teams, three from the Australasian group and one from the South African group. From the [[2018 Super Rugby season|2018 season]] the format changed again, with two South African teams and an Australian team being dropped. There were three conferences, one containing the five New Zealand teams, a South African one including Argentina's team and an Australian one including Japan's team. Due to the [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on sports#Rugby union|COVID-19 pandemic]] the competition had to undergo a change in structure and be split into regionalised tournaments. There were two national competitions, Australia's [[Super Rugby AU]] and New Zealand's [[Super Rugby Aotearoa]], and those were followed by [[Super Rugby Trans-Tasman]] in 2021, a crossover competition involving the five Australian sides playing the five New Zealand sides. Super Rugby currently only consists of Australian and New Zealand sides, with the Japanese [[Sunwolves]] departing the competition after the 2020 season, the South African sides voting to leave to join an expanded PRO14 (Later known as the [[United Rugby Championship]]), and the Argentine [[Jaguares (Super Rugby)|Jaguares]] not set to compete in any Super Rugby tournament in 2021. From 2022, the tournament reverted to round robin format featuring 12 teams, with the [[Fijian Drua]] and [[Moana Pasifika]] joining the competition. There are no divisions from 2022 onwards, with one main log being used instead, and top 8 teams qualifying for the playoffs. Since 2022, each Super Rugby season has featured a "Super Round", where an entire round of Super Rugby matches is played over a weekend at a single stadium; both the 2022 and 2023 Super Rounds were played at [[Melbourne Rectangular Stadium|AAMI Park]] in [[Melbourne]], with the 2024 Super Round set to be played there as well. == History == === {{anchor|Super10}}Background === Before 1996, a number of transnational competitions involving regional and provincial rugby union teams had taken shape in the southern hemisphere. The earliest of these was the [[South Pacific Championship]], which was launched in 1986 and continued until 1990. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:left;margin-left:1em;font-size:90%;float:right" |+ '''Super 6 Champions ''' ! style="width:50px;"| Season ! style="width:110px;"| Champions |- | style="text-align:center;"| [[South Pacific Championship#1992 Super 6|1992]] | [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] |} ==== Super 6 ==== After the demise of the South Pacific Championship, with no tournament played in 1991, the competition was relaunched as the [[South Pacific Championship#1992 Super 6|Super 6]] in 1992. The competition included three provincial teams from New Zealand: [[Auckland Rugby Union|Auckland]], [[Canterbury Rugby Football Union|Canterbury]], [[Wellington Rugby Football Union|Wellington]]; along with two Australian state teams: [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] and [[New South Wales Waratahs|New South Wales]]; and also the [[Fiji national rugby union team|Fiji national team]]. ==== Super 10 ==== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:left;margin-left:1em;font-size:90%;float:right" |+ '''Super 10 Champions 1993 – 1995''' ! style="width:50px;"| Season ! style="width:110px;"| Champions |- | style="text-align:center;"| [[Super 10 (rugby union)#1993 season|1993]] | [[Golden Lions|Transvaal]] |- | style="text-align:center;"| [[Super 10 (rugby union)#1994 season|1994]] | [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] |- | style="text-align:center;"| [[Super 10 (rugby union)#1995 season|1995]] | [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] |} {{Main|Super 10 Rugby}} In 1993, the Super Six competition was revamped and expanded into the Super 10 tournament. With [[Sporting boycott of South Africa during the apartheid era#End of apartheid|South Africa being readmitted into international sport]] following the dismantling of apartheid, there was an opportunity to launch an expanded competition which would also feature South Africa's top provincial teams. The inaugural competition featured the following teams: [[Waikato Rugby Union|Waikato]], [[Auckland Rugby Union|Auckland]], [[Otago Rugby Football Union|Otago]] and [[North Harbour Rugby Union|North Harbour]] (New Zealand); [[Sharks (rugby union)|Natal]], [[Bulls (rugby union)|Northern Transvaal]] and [[Lions (United Rugby Championship)|Transvaal]] (South Africa); [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] and [[New South Wales Waratahs|New South Wales]] (Australia) and [[Samoa national rugby union team|Western Samoa]] ([[Pacific Tri-Nations]] winner). The Super 10 was won by [[Lions (United Rugby Championship)|Transvaal]] (South Africa) in 1993, and by [[Queensland Reds|Queensland]] (Australia) in 1994 and 1995. === SANZAR era === ==== Super 12 (1995–2005) ==== The official declaration of professionalism in rugby union in August 1995 led to a restructuring of the Super 10 competition. Following the success of the [[1995 Rugby World Cup|1995 World Cup]], the rugby boards of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa formed SANZAR (South African, New Zealand and Australian Rugby) to administer an annual 12-team provincial/franchise based competition pitting regional teams from the three nations against each other. In addition it was decided to hold an annual [[Tri Nations Series|Tri-Nations Test Series]] between the three countries. A significant reason for the development of the Super 12 was the threat to [[rugby union]] from rival football code [[rugby league]]: part of the business model for the Foxtel pay TV network in Australia was to attract subscribers by offering an exclusive product (such as rugby union) which could not be seen on free-to-air broadcast television. By setting up the Super 12, the Unions had a product that was in demand from viewers, enabling them to sell a 10-year contract for exclusive television rights to News Corp for US$555 million, giving them both coverage and financial support to kickstart the new competition.{{cite web | title=More for players in new SANZAR deal | publisher=worldcupweb.com | url=http://www.worldcupweb.com/WCrugby/item.asp?NewsID=845 | access-date=17 July 2006 | archive-date=20 March 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060320101141/http://www.worldcupweb.com/WCrugby/item.asp?NewsID=845 | url-status=dead }} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;margin-left:1em;float:right" |+ Format history |- ! ([[Super Rugby AU|AU]], [[Super Rugby Aotearoa|NZ]], [[Super Rugby Trans-Tasman|TT]]) | 10 | [[Rugby Australia|Australia]], [[New Zealand Rugby|New Zealand]] |- | {{nowrap|2022–2024}} | rowspan=3| Super Rugby Pacific | 12 | rowspan=2| [[Rugby Australia|Australia]], [[Fiji Rugby Union|Fiji]], [[New Zealand Rugby|New Zealand]], [[List of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific Islands]] |- | {{nowrap|2025–2026}} | 11 |- | {{nowrap|2027–}} | 10 | [[Rugby Australia|Australia]], [[Fiji Rugby Union|Fiji]], [[New Zealand Rugby|New Zealand]] |} With significant sponsorship, and rugby turning a professional sport in August 1995, the Super 12 competition successfully kicked off in [[1996 Super 12 season|1996]] with five New Zealand franchises, four South African provinces and three domestic Australian teams competing. New Zealand's dominance of the competition began in the first year when the [[Blues (Super Rugby)|Auckland Blues]] won the inaugural competition defeating South African side the {{Rut|Sharks}} 45–21 in a home final. The Blues would repeat the success of 1996 beating Australian side the [[Brumbies|ACT Brumbies]] 23–7 in the [[1997 Super 12 season|1997]] final. The Blues then reached their third successive final in [[1998 Super 12 season|1998]] but went down to fellow countrymen the [[Crusaders (rugby union)|Canterbury Crusaders]] 13–20. This would mark the beginning of the Crusaders' three-year dominance as they went on to win the [[1999 Super 12 season|1999]] and [[2000 Super 12 season|2000]] finals over the [[Highlanders (rugby union)|Otago Highlanders]] and [[Brumbies|ACT Brumbies]] respectively. The [[2001 Super 12 season|2001 season]] was the first in which no New Zealand franchise reached the final, being contested between the [[Brumbies|ACT Brumbies]] and {{Rut|Sharks}} with the Brumbies convincing winners, with a 36–6 score line. The Crusaders won their 4th final in [[2002 Super 12 season|2002]] winning all 11 matches and missed out on their 5th in [[2003 Super 12 season|2003]] with a four-point loss to fellow countrymen the Blues. In [[2004 Super 12 season|2004]] the Brumbies took revenge on their 2000 final loss to the Crusaders defeating them 47–38 in front of a home crowd. The Crusaders would bounce back to win the [[2005 Super 12 season|2005]] final 35–25 against the Australian side the [[New South Wales Waratahs]] who reached their first-ever final. This was the last year of the 12 team format. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the [[Rugby Australia|Australian Rugby Union]] (ARU) had been pushing for a fourth Australian team to enter the competition, based in either [[Melbourne]] or [[Perth]]. News reports also alluded to a potential format re-structuring alongside expansion, to a 20-team competition.{{cite news |last=Growden |first=Greg |date=12 February 1999 |title=Super 12 is super right now – so don't meddle with it |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sydney-morning-herald-super-12-is-su/194364153/ |page=37 |work=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |publisher=[[Fairfax Media]] |via=[[Newspapers.com]] }} In early 2000, the ARU moved to quash a prospective joint bid for a new Australian Super 12 franchise, which had proposed to stage matches across both Melbourne and Perth by the unions in their respective states.{{cite news |last=Growden |first=Greg |date=2 February 2000 |title=Super 12 expansion push fails but the fight goes on |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sydney-morning-herald-super-12-expan/194364277/ |page=38 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=Fairfax Media |via=Newspapers.com }} The ARU stated that it preferred a potential new Australian team to be based in one capital city. Expansion into Australia at this time was viewed favourably by the [[South African Rugby Union]] (SARU), whereas [[New Zealand Rugby]] (NZR) was firmly against. [[Western Sydney]] later became a location for potential expansion, with three major [[rugby league]] clubs in the [[National Rugby League]] ([[Parramatta Eels]], [[Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs]], [[Penrith Panthers]]) aiming to be financial partners in a fourth Australian franchise.{{cite news |last=Growden |first=Greg |date=9 February 2001 |title=League wants slice of expanded Super 12 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sydney-morning-herald-league-wants-s/194364390/ |page=38 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=Fairfax Media |via=Newspapers.com }}{{cite news |date=16 February 2001 |title=Push for Super 12 team in city's west |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sydney-morning-herald-push-for-super/194364412/ |page=38 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=Fairfax Media |via=Newspapers.com }} Any expansion plans were not expected to take place until at least 2003,{{cite news |date=12 July 2001 |title=Super boost as Wallabies tackle AFL, league |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-sydney-morning-herald-super-boost-as/194364459/ |page=46 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=Fairfax Media |via=Newspapers.com }} with a fifth South African team also possible. On 11 December 2004, the [[Perth]]-based [[Western Force]] were admitted into the competition as a new franchise after receiving the endorsement of the ARU over a Melbourne-based franchise bid.{{cite news |date=10 December 2004 |title=Perth wins Super 14 berth |url=http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2004/12/10/1102625514090.html |url-status=dead |work=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |publisher=Fairfax Media |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041212015123/http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2004/12/10/1102625514090.html |archive-date=12 December 2004 }}{{cite news |date=11 December 2004 |title=Nervous wait over, it's party time in Perth |url=http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2004/12/10/1102625530725.html |url-status=dead |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=Fairfax Media |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041212021643/http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2004/12/10/1102625530725.html |archive-date=12 December 2004 }} In April the following year, the [[Bloemfontein]]-based [[Cheetahs (rugby union)|Cheetahs]] were announced as the fifth South African franchise to join the competition.{{cite news |date=16 April 2005 |title=Fifth South African Super 14 team named |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2005-04-16/fifth-south-african-super-14-team-named/1552760 |work=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]] }} The Cheetahs, composed of the Free State, [[Griquas (rugby union)|Griqualand West]] and [[Griffons (rugby union)|Griffons Rugby Union]]s, were awarded the franchise ahead of the Southern and Eastern Cape delegation, which had the support of the South African Sports Minister [[Makhenkesi Stofile]]. Both new franchises were admitted into the competition in the [[2006 Super 14 season|2006 season]]. ==== Super 14 (2006–2010) ==== SANZAR announced in December 2004 that a new five-year television deal had been signed that would cover 2006 to 2010, with [[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]] winning the rights for the UK, Australia and New Zealand, and [[SuperSport (South African TV channel)|SuperSport]] winning rights for South Africa. The contract was worth US$323 million over five years, a 16% annual increase compared to the previous deal. It covers international fixtures as well as the Super 14. SANZAR remained free to negotiate separate deals for other markets, such as France, Japan and the Americas. Under the new deal, Australia and South Africa each got one extra team in the competition, and a third round of fixtures was added to the Tri Nations Series. The new Australian team in the competition was based in [[Perth]] and was named the [[Western Force]]. The addition of the new South African team led to considerable controversy, including government involvement. Finally, the five teams for 2006 were confirmed to be the country's existing four teams plus the [[Cheetahs (rugby union)|Cheetahs]], which draws its players from the [[Free State Province|Free State]] and [[Northern Cape Province]]s. For the 2007 season, the [[Southern Spears]], based in [[Port Elizabeth, Eastern Cape|Port Elizabeth]], were originally intended to replace the lowest-finishing South African team from the 2006 competition. However, the existing South African Super 14 franchises opposed the plan, which was pushed through by controversial president of the [[South African Rugby Union]], Brian van Rooyen. After van Rooyen was ousted as president, SARU announced that the Spears would not enter the competition.{{cite web | url=http://152.111.1.87/argief/berigte/dieburger/2006/04/20/KS/23/spt-spears23.html | title=Spears kom straks met regsaksie | work=Die Burger | date=20 April 2006 | access-date=18 October 2015 | language=af | archive-date=5 January 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160105133916/http://152.111.1.87/argief/berigte/dieburger/2006/04/20/KS/23/spt-spears23.html | url-status=dead }} SARU investigated the viability of the Spears after discovering serious financial irregularities.{{cite web | url=http://152.111.1.87/argief/berigte/dieburger/2006/03/27/DB/2/spears27.html | title=Spears se baas wil vir oulaas pleit | work=Die Burger | date=27 March 2006 | access-date=18 October 2015 | language=af | archive-date=5 January 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160105133916/http://152.111.1.87/argief/berigte/dieburger/2006/03/27/DB/2/spears27.html | url-status=dead }} A [[High Court of South Africa]] ruling stated that the Spears had a valid contract to compete in the Super 14 and Currie Cup. However, because of the organisation's financial and administrative troubles, in November 2006 a settlement was reached. The Spears abandoned their legal case, and will continue to exist, but not compete in the Super 14.{{cite news | work=Planet Rugby | title=Spears abandon their Super conquest | url=http://www.planet-rugby.com/Teams/South_Africa/story_55239.shtml | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120912014430/http://www.planet-rugby.com/Teams/South_Africa/story_55239.shtml | url-status=dead | archive-date=12 September 2012 | date=16 November 2006 | access-date=22 November 2006 }} SANZAR rejected a proposal to split the Super 14 into two seven-team divisions, and decided to keep the competition in its traditional single-table format. Argentina and the Pacific Islands remained shut out of the competition. The two new teams did not perform all that well, the South African franchise the Cheetahs did the better of the two teams finishing 10th on the ladder notching up 5 season wins. The Australian franchise the Western Force only managed one victory and ended winning the wooden spoon as last placed 14th. The highlight for the Force was a 23-all draw against eventual champions the Crusaders, who defeated first-time finalists the [[Hurricanes (rugby union)|Hurricanes]] 19–12. [[File:Skrum.jpg|thumb|The Cats (now the Lions) playing the Sharks.]] During the 2007 season, 22 [[All Blacks]] missed the competition's first seven rounds as part of an All Black "conditioning programme" that was a part of the All Blacks' [[2007 Rugby World Cup]] preparations, and every New Zealand franchise was without players for the first seven rounds.{{cite news|title=All Blacks pulled out of the Super 14 |url=http://www.planet-rugby.com/Story/0,18259,3562_1692051,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929120504/http://www.planet-rugby.com/Story/0,18259,3562_1692051,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=29 September 2007 |publisher=planet-rugby.com |date=20 August 2006 |access-date=24 January 2007 }}{{cite news |title=Henry reveals his 'World Cup team' |url=http://www.planet-rugby.com/Story/0,18259,3562_1692085,00.html |publisher=planet-rugby.com |date=11 September 2006 |access-date=24 January 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080228193636/http://www.planet-rugby.com/Story/0%2C18259%2C3562_1692085%2C00.html |archive-date=28 February 2008 }}{{cite news| last=Leggat| first=David|title=Getting the balance in Super 14|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/section/story.cfm?c_id=4&ObjectID=10402597 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date=22 September 2006 |access-date=24 September 2006}} At the end of the regular season, for the first time since 1998, no Australian franchise had made the semi-finals. Although the Brumbies were strong and the Western Force experienced vast improvement, it was a poor season for the [[Queensland Reds]] and [[New South Wales Waratahs|Waratahs]] who finished last and second last respectively. Also, the competition featured the first all-South African final as the [[Sharks (rugby union)|Sharks]] and [[Bulls (rugby union)|Bulls]], who finished 1–2 on the season ladder, both won their respective semi-finals. The final, held [[Kings Park Stadium|in Durban]], saw the visiting Bulls win 20–19. During the time the competition was branded as the Super 14, only two teams won the tournament. The Crusaders winning the 2006 and 2008 tournaments; while the Bulls ended victorious in 2007, 2009, and 2010 respectively. ==== Super Rugby: 15 teams (2011–2015) ==== SANZAR unveiled in 2009 its model for an expanded season that would begin in 2011. This model was based around the original ARU proposal for three national conferences: each side were to have played the other four teams from their own country twice and the other ten teams once each; the season has to end with a six-team finals series. There were four major compromises, however, designed to accommodate certain wishes of each country, that somewhat complicated the model: * Each team would only play four, instead of all five, teams in each of the other two national conferences, making sixteen regular season games for each team instead of eighteen, and allowing for a late February start, somewhat placating the ARU and NZRU who wanted a March start. * There would be a three-week gap for the June test (international) matches favoured by the SARU. * The season would finish in early August so as not to overlap new streamlined versions of New Zealand's and South Africa's domestic competitions. * The three conference winners and the three best performers of the remaining teams would qualify for a three-week finals series, with seedings deciding the match-ups. This system is a hybrid of the conference-based qualification system favoured by the SARU and the 'top six' model favoured by the ARU and NZRU. SANZAR announced in 2009 the addition of a fifth Australian team that would play in the expanded "Super Rugby" competition in 2011. The licence was awarded to [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], Australia, and the team's name announced as the [[Melbourne Rebels]]. The Australian start-up franchise was given the nod ahead of South Africa's [[Southern Kings]].{{cite web|last=Walton |first=Darren |url=http://www.foxsports.com.au/story/0,8659,26339154-5002381,00.html |title=Melbourne granted Super licence | Super Rugby |work=Fox Sports |date=12 November 2009 |access-date=23 February 2012}} Brian Waldron, former CEO of the [[National Rugby League|NRL]] club the [[Melbourne Storm]], was confirmed as the new CEO of the Rebels on 11 January 2010, but resigned on 23 April after a [[Melbourne Storm salary cap breach|salary cap breach]] was uncovered at the Storm.{{cite news|url=http://www.smh.com.au/rugby-union/union-news/rebels-act-swiftly-in-asking-waldron-to-clear-his-desk-20100422-tg62.html | title=Melbourne Storm salary cap scandal|last=Rakic |first=Josh |date=23 April 2010 | work =The Sydney Morning Herald |access-date=23 April 2010}} === SANZAAR era === ==== Expansion: 18 teams (2016–2017) ==== In February 2012, SANZAR chief executive Greg Peters announced that the organisation was considering adding franchises in Argentina, Japan and the United States in 2016, the first year of SANZAR's next television contract. This was also the year that [[rugby sevens]] [[Rugby union at the Summer Olympics|entered the Olympics]], which contributed towards increased interest in the sport in many countries, including Japan and the US.{{cite news|url=http://www.dailytelegraph.com.au/sport/rugby-gold/super-rugby-going-global/story-fn8ti7yn-1226268126917 |title=Super Rugby going global |first=Jamie |last=Pandaram |work=Sydney Daily Telegraph |date=11 February 2012 |access-date=19 February 2011}} Australian sports broadcasting analyst Colin Smith noted that the addition of Japanese and American teams could result in a TV deal worth more than [[Australian dollar|A$]]1 billion beyond 2020. Specifically, he stated, "You could have a deal comparable to the other major sports in Australia. Rugby is [[Rugby union in the United States|a college (university) sport in the US]], if soccer can create [[Major League Soccer|its own league]] there and sell teams for $40 million, imagine what you could do in 10–12 years with rugby in that market." By comparison, the largest TV deal in Australian sport, that of the [[Australian Football League]] ([[Australian rules football|Australian rules]]), is worth A$1.26 billion from 2012 to 2016. Even that figure was dwarfed by the [[NFL on television|TV contracts]] of the [[National Football League|NFL]], for which contracts at the time were worth more than US$4 billion annually.{{cite web|url=http://www.sanzarrugby.com/sanzar-news/absolute-possibilities-for-sanzar-expansion-says-peters/ |title="Absolute Possibilities" for SANZAR Expansion Says Peters |first=James |last=Mortimer |publisher=SANZAR |date=11 February 2012 |access-date=19 February 2012}} Peters added that the conference-based structure was ideal for expanding the competition to new territories, either by adding new conferences or by adding teams to the current conferences. He also discussed the possibility that offshore Super Rugby teams could be a home for surplus players from the SANZAR countries, keeping them in the SANZAR fold and away from European clubs.{{cite news|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/sunday-star-times/latest-edition/6443422/Time-may-be-right-for-Sanzar-to-expand-Super-Rugby |title=Time may be right for Sanzar to expand Super Rugby |first=Duncan |last=Johnstone |work=The Sunday Star-Times |date=19 February 2012 |access-date=19 February 2012}} Prior to Super Rugby's broadcast contracts expiring after the 2015 season, SANZAR considered several alternatives for the competition's future organisation: {{cite news | url=http://www.smh.com.au/rugby-union/union-news/sanzar-considering-splitting-super-rugby-in-2016-20130726-2qpu8.html | title=SANZAR considering splitting Super Rugby in 2016 | work=Sydney Morning Herald | date=27 July 2013 | access-date=26 August 2013 | last=Robinson | first=Georgina}} * Retention of the conference system that was in place for 2011–15. * Expansion of the structure to include teams from Asia, the United States and/or Canada.{{cite news | url=http://www.espnscrum.com/super-rugby-2013/rugby/story/195973.html | title=Super Rugby to consider expansion | work=ESPN Scrum | date=27 August 2013 | access-date=27 August 2013}} * A split of the competition, with South Africa forming one competition with the likely addition of at least one Argentine side, and Australia and New Zealand forming another, with the possibility of including Asian teams. On 24 June 2026, following the conclusion of the [[2026 Super Rugby Pacific season|2026 season]], [[New Zealand Rugby]] (NZR), the licence holder of [[Moana Pasifika]]'s Super Rugby team, confirmed the club's withdrawal from the competition.{{cite news |last=Worthington |first=Sam |date=24 June 2026 |title=‘Unfortunate’ news as next Super Rugby comp takes shape |url=https://www.nine.com.au/sport/rugby/super-pacific-2026-news-moana-pasifika-exit-confirmed-10-team-competition-next-season-20260624-p609jy.html |work=[[Nine.com.au]] |publisher=Nine Entertainment |access-date=26 June 2026 }} It was indicated, however, that a return to Super Rugby in 2028 remained a possibility.{{cite episode |credits=Ewart, Richard (presenter) |url=https://www.abc.net.au/pacific/programs/pacificbeat/rugbymoanademise/106839262 |title=Could Moana Pasifika's phoenix rise from the Super Rugby ashes in two years' time? |series=Pacific Beat |station=[[ABC Australia (Asia-Pacific TV channel)|ABC Pacific]] |network=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] |air-date=25 June 2026 }} == Franchises == === Current franchises === {{Main|Super Rugby franchise areas}} There are eleven franchises currently in Super Rugby; four from Australia, one from Fiji, five from New Zealand, and one representing the Pacific Islands. Each franchise is representing a franchise area, with each franchise in New Zealand representing a collection of unions, compared to the Australian model of one franchise per union. This model differs from the traditional club-based model of other Australian sports; with 4 Super Rugby teams in Australia compared to the 16 Australian-based [[National Rugby League]] teams and the 18 teams of the [[Australian Football League]]. However the Australian Super Rugby salary cap stands greater than the [[A-League Men|A-League]], the [[Big Bash League|BBL]] and the [[National Basketball League (Australia)|NBL]].{{cn|date=December 2024}} == Brand and image == === Logo === During the last season of the Super 12, Coast Design of Sydney was commissioned to design a new logo for the Super 14.{{cite web| url=http://www.coastdesign.com.au/pages/s14.htm |title=Super 14 |access-date=28 January 2007 |publisher=coastdesign.com.au |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061208173314/http://www.coastdesign.com.au/pages/s14.htm |archive-date = 8 December 2006}} The Super 14 logo broke away from the traditional shield formats, common to many sporting codes, and used Roman numerals (XIV), which is unique for sport in the region.{{cite news| url=http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2005/08/22/1124562783752.html |title=SANZAR launches Super 14 logo |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=22 August 2005 |access-date=18 January 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070321102252/http://www.rugbyheaven.smh.com.au/articles/2005/08/22/1124562783752.html |archive-date=21 March 2007}} The game's dynamism and speed are suggested by the orbiting football which has three distinct stitches, a subtle reference to the three countries of the tournament. The Super Rugby logo dispenses with numbers, featuring a large blue "S" with a white rugby ball in the centre and "S{{smallcaps|upe}}R{{smallcaps|ugb}}Y" below the "S". The three stitches of the previous ball are retained. Before the expansion to the Super 14, the Super 12 used a logo in the shape of a shield, which had the sponsors name at the top, and then the words "Rugby" and "Super 12". The lower half of the logo used three different coloured stripes, green, black and gold, the respective colours of the national teams of South Africa, New Zealand and Australia.{{cite web |url=http://itip.com.au/s12-1999/index.html |title=1999 Super 12 |publisher=itip.com.au |access-date=23 February 2012 |archive-date=6 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606090239/http://itip.com.au/s12-1999/index.html |url-status=dead }} === Naming rights === The [[naming rights]] for the competition are different in the five countries: * In New Zealand, [[Investec Bank]] has naming rights starting with the 2011 season, and the competition is referred to as '''Investec Super Rugby'''. During the Super 14 era, [[sporting goods]] retailer [[Rebel (company)|Rebel Sport]] had naming rights and the Super 14 competition was referred to as the '''Rebel Sport Super 14'''. Previously the naming rights holders were [[U-Bix]] and then [[Spark New Zealand|Telecom New Zealand (TNZ)]]. Telecom used its ISP brand Xtra as the label in their last year of holding naming rights. * In Australia, telecommunications company [[Vodafone Hutchison Australia|Vodafone]] has been the title sponsor of Super Rugby since 2017{{cite web|url=https://www.rugby.com.au/news/2017/02/13/00/10/super-rugby-vodafone |title=Vodafone return as naming rights partner of Super Rugby |access-date=21 February 2014}} As a result, the competition is officially referred to as '''Vodafone Super Rugby'''. Prior to this, Super Rugby in Australia was sponsored by [[Suncorp Group]] through their life insurance brand [[Asteron Life]]. Vodafone were also the title sponsor of the competition during the Super 12 era. In the first season of Super Rugby, Australia had no naming rights partner. Previous to that, Investec acquired naming rights in the middle of the Super 14 era from [[Lion Nathan]], who had named the competition the ''Tooheys New Super 14'', after its [[Tooheys New]] beer brand. *In South Africa, telecommunications carrier [[Vodacom]] has naming rights, and the expanded competition is referred to as '''Vodacom Super Rugby'''. Before 1999, when cigarette advertising was banned in South Africa, the competition was sponsored by [[Winfield (cigarette)|Winfield]]. *In Argentina, telecommunications carrier [[Telecom Argentina|Personal]] has naming rights, and the expanded competition is referred to as '''Personal Super Rugby'''. *In Japan, real estate developer [[Mitsubishi Estate]] acquired naming rights in 2018, the competition referred to as '''Mitsubishi Estate Super Rugby'''.{{cite web|url=http://www.mec.co.jp/e/news/pdf/mec180222_superrugby.pdf|title=Mitsubishi Estate scores a try to become the Sponsor of 2018 Super Rugby Title Sponsor|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180224113616/http://www.mec.co.jp/e/news/pdf/mec180222_superrugby.pdf|archive-date=24 February 2018|url-status=live}} The competition had no title sponsor in Japan during the 2016 and 2017 seasons. == Competition records == {{Main|List of Super Rugby records}} === Team records === ==== Single match ==== * '''Highest score:''' 96 points – Crusaders defeated Waratahs 96–19, 2002 * '''Highest combined score:''' 137 points – Chiefs defeated Lions 72–65, 2010 * '''Lowest combined score:''' 6 points – Highlanders defeated Crusaders 6–0, 2009 * '''Highest winning margin:''' 89 points – Bulls defeated Reds 92–3, 2007 * '''Most tries in a match by both teams:''' 18 by Lions and Chiefs, 2010 * '''Most tries in a match by one team:''' 14 by Crusaders (v Waratahs), 2002; [[Macca Springer]], Crusaders, 2025 * '''Conversions:''' 13 – [[Andrew Mehrtens]], Crusaders, 2002 * '''Penalties:''' 9 – [[Elton Jantjies]], Lions, 2012 == Domestic competitions == Each respective country competing in Super Rugby has a number of their own domestic leagues, which feed into Super Rugby teams. In New Zealand, the [[National Provincial Championship (2006–present)|National Provincial Championship]] is the most prominent domestic competition below the Super Rugby, in which all the respective Unions are also aligned with Super Rugby sides. In Australia, there have been several domestic competitions, the most successful iteration so far being the [[National Rugby Championship]] (NRC), which was launched in 2014 and ran for five seasons before being cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Several teams that played in the former [[Australian Rugby Championship]] in 2007,{{cite web | title=Mazda Australian Rugby Championship | url=http://www.rugby.com.au/fixtures_results/australian_rugby_championship/overview,50381.html | publisher=Australian Rugby Union | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070603204109/http://www.rugby.com.au/fixtures_results/australian_rugby_championship/overview,50381.html | archive-date=3 June 2007 | df=dmy-all }} were revived for the NRC. In 2025, the concept was revived with the launch of a new domestic competition, [[Super Rugby AUS]], which runs alongside the U19s and U16s competitions. Argentina, until 2018, like South Africa and New Zealand, had a national championship where several provincial unions competed, the [[Campeonato Argentino]]. Another national championship, but for clubs, is [[Nacional de Clubes]]. Japan's main domestic competition was the [[Japan Rugby League One]] (formerly Top League), featuring 16 clubs, while the second division, the [[Top Challenge League]], featured 8 clubs. Fiji's domestic competition is the [[Skipper Cup]], featuring the countries top 12 provincial sides. == Media == Until 2020, in Australia, pay TV station [[Fox Sports (Australia)|Fox Sports]] showed every match live and beginning in 2016, free-to-air station [[Network Ten]] started showing a full match replay every Sunday morning of the 'Match of the Round' featuring at least one Australian team. Network Ten also showed full match replays of all finals matches featuring Australian teams. From 2021 onwards, [[Nine Network]] possesses the broadcasting rights, and any future Super Rugby seasons will have games aired live on streaming service [[Stan (streaming service)|Stan]], with the potential for a number of games to be simulcast live on either Nine's flagship free-to-air channel or a multichannel, similar to the current situation with [[Super Rugby AU]].{{Cite web|last=Phillips|first=Sam|date=9 November 2020|title=Nine, Rugby Australia confirm groundbreaking $100m broadcast deal|url=https://www.smh.com.au/sport/rugby-union/nine-rugby-australia-confirm-groundbreaking-100m-broadcast-deal-20201109-p56csm.html|access-date=2 December 2020|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}} Super Rugby is broadcast on [[Supersport (TV channel)|Supersport]] in South Africa and is [[simulcast]] terrestrially on [[M-Net]]. [[SKY Sport (New Zealand)|Sky Sport]] is the official broadcaster in New Zealand. Super Rugby was broadcast in over 40 countries – in the UK on [[Sky Sports]]; in Spain it is broadcast by [[Digital+]], and in the United States by [[ESPN+]], which has confirmed all matches will be broadcast live or on demand. In Canada, [[The Sports Network|TSN]] broadcasts all matches only on TSN GO, their online [[Standard-definition television|SD]] streaming platform. iterations of the Super Rugby trophy awarded to the winner of the Super Rugby competitions. The Super 14 trophy, unveiled in New Zealand ahead of the [[2006 Super 14 season|2006 season]], was made of sterling silver with the competition logo on a globe sitting atop of a four-sided twisted spiral.{{cite web |url=https://www.jenshansen.com/blogs/blog-news-press/10657441-rugby-trophy-commissions |title=Media Release |publisher=jenshansen.com |date=8 February 2006 |access-date=28 January 2007 |archive-date=25 January 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070125014741/http://www.jenshansen.com/news/super14.aspx |url-status=dead }} Jens Hansen Gold and Silversmith in [[Nelson, New Zealand]] hand-made the trophy which took over two months to complete. On 30 June 2011, [[SANZAAR|SANZAR]] unveiled the new trophy that would be presented to the winners of the Super Rugby final from [[2011 Super Rugby season|2011]] and beyond.{{cite web|url=http://www.sport24.co.za/Rugby/Super15/SANZAR-unveils-new-S15-trophy-20110630 |title=Sport 24 |publisher=Sport 24 |access-date=23 February 2012}} It was crafted from solid stainless steel and polished to a mirror finish, and stood at a height of 65 cm with an overall mass of 18 kilograms. The trophy was designed by Blue Sky Design of [[Sydney]]. The trophy was manufactured by Box and Dice Pty Ltd also based in Sydney. SANZAR CEO Greg Peters stated that "the shape of the trophy is centred around three curved legs, each representing the Conferences involved in the Super Rugby competition... The champions trophy is the 'big one', and will become the ultimate symbol of Super Rugby supremacy in the years to come." The colour on each leg corresponds to the Conferences with gold for Australia, black for New Zealand, and green for South Africa. === Player of the Year === The Player of the Year award was announced in 2025 as the premier individual honour in Super Rugby Pacific.{{cite web |title=Super Rugby Pacific introduces Player of the Year award |url=https://super.rugby/superrugby/news/super-rugby-pacific-introduces-player-of-the-year-award/ |date=4 February 2025 |website=super.rugby |publisher=SANZAAR }} Votes are awarded on a 3–2–1 basis in each regular season match by team captains and coaches, supplemented by a panel of rugby media representatives from Australia, New Zealand and Fiji. Voting results are publicly released each week until Round 10, after which they are kept confidential until the end of the season. The final standings not only determine the Player of the Year winner but also help inform the selection of the new [[#Team of the Year|Team of the Year]], while also underpinning eligibility for the [[#Rookie of the Year|Rookie of the Year]] award. One of the cited reasons for the introduction of the Player of the Year award was aimed to make Super Rugby more attractive to fans.{{cite news |date=12 February 2025 |title=Super Rugby Pacific returns with a Lions tour looming large |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-02-12/super-rugby-returns-with-a-lions-tour-looming-large/104923826 |work=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]] }} The inaugural winner of the Player of the Year award was [[Moana Pasifika]]'s [[Ardie Savea]].{{cite web |title=Ardie Savea crowned 2025 Super Rugby Pacific Player of the Year |url=https://super.rugby/superrugby/news/ardie-savea-crowned-2025-super-rugby-pacific-player-of-the-year/ |date=18 May 2025 |website=super.rugby |publisher=SANZAAR |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250521185715/https://super.rugby/superrugby/news/ardie-savea-crowned-2025-super-rugby-pacific-player-of-the-year/ |archive-date=21 May 2025 }} Savea accrued 42 points across the season, eleven points clear of second-place [[Tom Hooper (rugby union)|Tom Hooper]]. {| class="wikitable plainrowheaders" |+ List of Player of the Year winners ! Super Rugby is a men's professional rugby union club competition involving teams from Australia, Fiji, New Zealand, and the Pacific Islands. It has previously included teams from Argentina, Japan, and South Africa. Super Rugby started as the Super 12 in the 1996 season with 12 teams from Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa, building on competitions dating back to the South Pacific Championship in 1986. The Super 12 was established by SANZAR after the sport became professional in 1995. After the COVID-19 pandemic forced the competition to split into three, the reformed competition in 2021 only included teams from Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific islands.
The name was changed to Super 14 with the addition of two teams for the 2006 season, and with expansion to 15 teams for the 2011 season, the competition was rebranded as Super Rugby (with no number). In 2016 two new teams, the Jaguares from Argentina and Sunwolves from Japan, joined the competition, playing in two newly separated African groups. In 2018, the Cheetahs, Kings and Western Force were dropped, leaving 15 teams. The Sunwolves left the competition before the end of the 2020 season.
The 2020 season was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to international travel restrictions relating to the pandemic, Rugby Australia and New Zealand Rugby held domestic tournaments, Super Rugby AU and Super Rugby Aotearoa respectively. Both these tournaments continued in 2021, to be followed by Super Rugby Trans-Tasman, a crossover tournament. In September 2020, the South African Rugby Union withdrew their four franchises from the competition, with plans for them to join the PRO14. The Argentine Jaguares also left the competition.
In August 2021 a 12-team format was confirmed, with the addition of the Fijian Drua and Moana Pasifika, a team representing the Pacific Islands. The tournament from 2022 is named Super Rugby Pacific.
The competition has been dominated by New Zealand teams, who have won 21 times in 28 years. The Crusaders have won most often, with 13 titles.
